Welcome to Words of Plainness
March 31, 2026
by Brother Aaron
community
announcement
welcome
I want to begin the way I hope every encounter on this site begins—with honesty.
This ministry exists because Jesus Christ changed my life, and I believe He wants to change yours. Not through argument. Not through pressure. Through encounter. Through the kind of meeting that happens when a person sets aside what they think they know and asks, with a willing heart, Who are you, really?
That is the question at the center of everything here.
What This Place Is
Words of Plainness is an interfaith Christian witness. My brother James and I are members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, and we write from that tradition with full conviction. But we did not build this for an audience that already agrees with us. We built it for anyone who takes Jesus Christ seriously enough to sit with the scriptures, wrestle honestly with what they find there, and let the encounter do its work.
Seekers and saints find common ground here. That is not a slogan—it is the structural principle of everything we have written.
What You Will Find
The site is organized into two volumes. Volume 1: Christ-Centered Discipleship begins with the foundations of faith—how we come to know anything at all, how prayer works, what it means to receive Christ—and then moves into a thorough study of Christ's personal character and mortal ministry. From there, the journey opens into interactive discipleship practices: specific, concrete ways to follow Him, with commitments you choose at your own pace and depth.
Volume 2: Covenants & Theology presents the full systematic theology of the Restoration—from the nature of God and the spiritual creation to the Plan of Salvation and our eternal inheritance. Volume 2 arrives after Volume 1's shared ground, so that the distinctive claims of the Restoration gain weight from the fruit the reader has already witnessed.
Every chapter includes audio narration you can listen to as you read. While listening, paragraphs are highlighted in sync to the audio (not perfect but helpful). Many chapters include musical testimonies—original songs in a Sacred Americana tradition that carry the chapter's themes into worship. The lyrics and musical production of all songs were done by Brother Aaron. Study slides, downloadable PDFs, and interactive reflection tools are woven throughout. This is not a static reading experience. It is a place to encounter Christ and respond from your own faith and traditions.
What Is Coming
The site is alive and growing. New chapters are being authored and published regularly. The "Learn of Me" movement—a five-chapter study of Christ's life from prophecy through Resurrection—is complete. Discipleship Practices chapters are rolling out across six topical groups, from Christ's manifesto in the Sermon on the Mount through endurance and eternal perspective. The Restoration chapters and Volume 2 are on the horizon.
If you want to know when new content is published, subscribe to the newsletter at the bottom of any page.
How to Be Here
Read at your own pace. Use the reflection and journal tools built into every chapter—they are private to you unless you choose to share. If you are the kind of person who grows through conversation, join the Discord community where readers discuss what they are learning.
There is no proselytizing here. No sales funnel. No pressure. Just a willing heart and honest engagement with the person of Jesus Christ. That is enough. It has always been enough.
I am glad you are here.
In the name of Jesus Christ,
Brother Aaron

Who Is Brother Aaron?
April 1, 2026
by Brother Aaron
introduction
testimony
ministry
My name is Aaron Powner. I am a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, a husband, a father, and the chief author of all writings found at wordsofplainness.org
I call myself Brother Aaron because that is what I am—a brother in Christ to anyone willing to sit down and talk honestly about Him.
I carry the title Ministering Elder not as a credential but as a description of what I try to do. I minister. I serve. I bear witness. Not from a pulpit above anyone, but from a chair beside them. The word Elder in our tradition does not mean aged—it means one who has been given stewardship to teach and testify. That is the stewardship I have accepted, and Words of Plainness is how I carry it out.
Why This Ministry Exists
I did not set out to build a website. I set out to answer a question that would not leave me alone: If I truly believe what I say about Jesus Christ, what am I doing about it?
For years, my brother James and I had been writing together—working through the scriptures, wrestling with the theology we were raised with, trying to put into plain language what we had come to know. The project began as letters to our children, but the manuscript grew into numerous chapters. It sat on a shelf. The files were stored on a hard drive.
What changed was that I stopped asking whether I was ready and started asking whether the people who needed this work could afford to wait until I felt ready. The answer was no. So I built the site, recorded the chapters in my own voice, composed the music, and opened the door.
What I Believe
I believe Jesus Christ is the living Son of God. I believe He suffered, died, and rose again—not as metaphor, but as history. I believe we are saved by His grace. I also believe that His grace requires everything of us, and that this is not a burden but a rescue. I believe He stands at the door of every human heart and knocks, and that He has never once stopped knocking.
I believe the gospel was restored through the Prophet Joseph Smith, and that The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints carries the authority and ordinances of Christ's original Church. But I do not exclude anyone from faith in the Savior, and I think of all who seek Him as brothers and sisters in faith. I have no interest in arguing about who is right about Christ. I witness that Christ is right, and that is what matters to all who hunger and thirst after righteousness.
I write from that conviction without apology. I did not build this ministry for people who agree with me. I built it for anyone willing to encounter Christ with an honest heart and let the encounter do its work in their lives.
What Ministering Elder Means in Practice
It means I answer messages. It means I sit with people as equals (both in reality and in virtual reality) and talk about God for hours. It means I write chapters that take weeks because I will not publish a sentence I have not prayed over. It means I compose music at night in our camper and weep with joy over lyrics because the Spirit is in the room and I cannot pretend otherwise.
It means I do not argue. I witness. There is a difference. An argument tries to win. A witness simply tells the truth about what happened to me and trusts God with the result. That is the posture of this entire ministry—service before teaching, trust before doctrine, encounter before explanation.
An Invitation
If you have never visited Words of Plainness, I invite you to begin: www.wordsofplainness.org
Start with whatever chapter title catches your eye. Listen to the audio narration if you prefer hearing to reading. Sit with the reflection prompts. You will not be tracked, sold to, or pressured. You will simply be welcomed—as a seeker, a saint, or something in between.
My brother James and I wrote these things for you. Not for an audience. For you —the one reading this right now.
Come and see.
In the name of Jesus Christ,
Brother Aaron Powner
Ministering Elder and Chief Author
Words of Plainness

pages.title: We Know in Part
pages.text:
← Back to Posts
We Know in Part
April 29, 2026
by Brother Aaron
faith
scripture
discipleship
There is a phrase in Paul's first letter to the Corinthians that I have returned to more times than I can count: we know in part. Not we know nothing — Paul is not an agnostic. Not we know everything — Paul is not a fool. We know in part. Partially. Genuinely, but incompletely.
I find that the people who have the hardest time with questions of faith are often the ones who believe that certainty and faith are the same thing — that you either know everything or you know nothing worth standing on. Paul offers a different picture. The glass is real. The glass is dark. Both things are true at once.
I have built my ministry on this. Not on having all the answers. Not on performing a confidence I do not possess. But on what I do know, held plainly, and what I do not know, held honestly. Christ is real. He is the same yesterday, today, and forever. And He is patient with a man who still sees through a glass darkly.
That is enough to move forward in faith.
(1 Corinthians 13:9-12)

Now on Streaming — Words of Plainness: Musical Testimonies
May 9, 2026
by Brother Aaron
music
announcement
musical-testimonies
A small piece of news that means a great deal to me.
The first two singles from Words of Plainness: Musical Testimonies are now live on Spotify, Apple Music, YouTube Music, and iTunes. If you have a moment, give them a listen — and if either one finds a place in your week, save it, share it, or pass it along to someone who might need it.
The Marks of Your Worth — released March 16, 2026
This is the ministry anthem. It is a re-imagining of Come Thou Fount built around a covenant dialogue: the disciple speaks, and the Savior answers. The line that the whole song turns on is His, not ours — the marks of your worth are still upon Me . He has not forgotten what it cost to claim us. He carries the receipt.
I released this one on March 16 because that was my mother's birthday. She is the first person who taught me that I was loved before I had done anything to deserve it, and the song is a small offering back to that grace.
Three things the song confesses, plainly:
Christ calls each of us by name — not by category, not in a crowd
The marks of His Atonement are enduring witnesses of every soul's worth
Salvation is relational before it is spatial — heaven begins in the redeemed heart
Listen: Spotify · Apple Music · iTunes · YouTube
The First One I Turn To — released May 9, 2026
The first of the chapter testimonies to arrive on streaming. It belongs to Chapter 14 of the ministry — Prayer as a Lifestyle — the chapter every other discipleship practice on the site is built on.
The title is the thesis. Prayer was never meant to be a performance, and it was never meant to be reserved for emergencies. It is the first direction the heart turns when there is nowhere else worth turning. Some days it is the only honest thing I have to offer. Some days it is enough.
If you have ever felt like prayer was something you were not doing right, this song is for you. If you have ever found the quiet middle of a long morning to be the place God was waiting all along, this song is for you too.
Listen: Spotify · Apple Music · iTunes · YouTube
What this catalog is, and what it isn't
Words of Plainness: Musical Testimonies is the music side of the ministry. Each chapter on this site eventually receives a song that distills its central testimony — not a summary, but a witness. The song says, in plainness, what the chapter took longer to say in prose.
Two songs are out today. More will follow as the chapters that carry them are completed. If a song lands somewhere it was needed, that is the whole reason it exists.
If you would like to support the music traveling further, the most useful things you can do are simple: save the songs to your library on the platform you use, add them to a playlist if they fit, and share them with someone you trust. The streaming services pay attention to those signals more than any other.
Thank you for listening. Thank you for being here.
— Aaron

pages.title: Approaches to Belief
pages.text:
Approaches to Belief
"Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord." Isaiah 1:18
This is not an argument. It is a map.
Somewhere on it is the place you actually stand — not the place someone assumed you stand, and not the place you would be assigned by the label you happen to carry.
Whatever you believe when you arrive here, you are welcome. Theist, atheist, agnostic, or genuinely unsure — every one of those positions is argued in this resource by its own best reasons, sourced to the thinkers who actually made them. Including the objections mine has to answer.
Seven sections. Roughly forty minutes at a steady pace, or as long as you like. There is a reflection at the end of each one; nothing is graded, nothing is sent anywhere, and nothing is stored beyond your own browser.
Facilitator
Set the frame before advancing: nobody here is being converted; we are locating ourselves honestly.
If the group is mixed, say so out loud. It earns the room.
Arrow keys or Space advance. Press P to toggle Present mode.
Before we begin Where do I stand?
Two questions, not one
People collapse them constantly, and the collapse is the source of most bad conversations about faith.
The first is about belief : do you hold that deity exists? The second is about knowledge : do you claim to know it—and can you say what warrants the claim?
These are independent. A person can believe firmly and claim no certainty. A person can disbelieve and freely admit they cannot prove it. And knowing is more than believing hard; it is believing with a warrant you can point to. Section 1 asks what counts as one.
Place yourself where you actually are.
Not where you think you should be. Not where you would defend yourself if pressed.
This map does not measure what happens to you. It measures your present state, your intentions, and your leanings.
Click anywhere on the grid. The edges are the hard forms of each position; the center is the soft. The vertical axis is degree of belief—what you hold to be true. The horizontal axis is knowledge—the degree to which you claim to know it, and can give warrant for the claim.
Deity here means one or more. Christians themselves differ on how the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one. This map does not decide that question, and your placement should not have to either.
If you have never truly asked either question, you are not on this map yet. That is not a failing. It is a legitimate place to start, and this resource was written for you as much as for anyone.
Now—can you say why ?
Not why someone else holds your position. Why you do. If the answer comes quickly and in someone else's words, that is worth noticing.
And one harder question, which I used to put to laboratory students: how do you know what you don't know, when you don't know that you don't know it?
You can't—not alone. You need a witness outside your own faculties: another mind arguing honestly against you, or a faculty the ones you already trust do not include. The next four sections supply the first. Section 1 proposes the second.
Plato, Meno 80d.
Facilitator
Do not let anyone answer for someone else. Silence here is productive.
Ask aloud: what would have to be true for you to move one box in any direction?
Watch for people who place themselves where they think they ought to be. Name it gently.
Ask the twisty question and wait. Do not answer it. Collect two or three attempts, then advance.
Before we begin Where do I stand?
Four words, used carefully
Theist. Believes that deity exists—one or more.
Atheist. Does not believe that deity exists. This is a judgment, not an absence; Section 3 argues it by its own best reasons.
Agnostic. Does not claim to know. In its soft form: I do not know. In its hard form, Huxley's own: no one can know. Both live on the left half of the map.
Gnostic. Claims to know. In its soft form: I know, and I know that my knowing is partial. In its hard form: I know fully and certainly. Both live on the right half.
Notice what none of the four names: ignorance itself. Every position on this map has gaps. The map does not measure whether you have them. It measures how honest you are about them.
1 How We Come to Know
Before we compare answers, let us agree on what counts as knowing
Most arguments about God are actually arguments about evidence — conducted by people who never said out loud what they would accept as evidence. So let us do that part first.
Human beings gather knowledge along four natural paths.
The Senses What we perceive directly: seen, heard, touched, measured.
Establishes: the physical world, reliably and repeatably.
Cannot reach: anything leaving no physical trace — and cannot check its own accuracy without using itself.
Authority What we accept on the testimony of others: teachers, texts, institutions, experts.
Establishes: nearly everything any of us knows. You have not personally verified the speed of light.
Cannot reach: certainty beyond the reliability of the witness.
Reason What we derive by logic from what we already hold.
Establishes: consistency, valid inference, the exposure of contradiction.
Cannot reach: new premises. Reason processes; it does not originate.
Academic Intuition Conclusions arriving without conscious derivation, drawn from accumulated experience — the physicist who sees the answer before working it. A rational process, however mysterious it feels.
Establishes: insight faster than deliberation.
Cannot reach: past the experience it was built from.
These four together are the natural framework , and it is not defective. It functions precisely as designed for the questions it is equipped to address. Philosophy, the arts, and the sciences have yielded incalculable benefit to human life. Nothing here asks you to think less of them.
Facilitator
Press the authority card. Most people underestimate how much of what they "know" is testimony.
Good aside: which of these four did you use to get to work this morning? All four.
1 How We Come to Know
Three working axioms
To go further we need three assumptions. They cannot be proven — every framework rests on something unproven — but they are the ones science itself runs on.
1 · A shared reality We exist together in the same world.
2 · Genuine perception To some extent we perceive that reality, and our own nature within it.
3 · Sufficient uniformity Reality is regular enough to be explored with some degree of certainty — through patterns; cause and effect; scale, proportion, and quantity; systems and system models; energy and matter; structure and function; and stability and change .
Those seven are not improvised. They are the crosscutting concepts — the organizing principles the Next Generation Science Standards identify as the lenses through which every scientific discipline examines the natural world. I taught them in a public-school science laboratory for twenty-six years.
They are how a scientist actually reasons about anything. And they work just as well pointed at questions science does not usually ask.
NGSS Lead States, Next Generation Science Standards: For States, By States , Appendix G (2013).
1 How We Come to Know
What truth is
Philosophy offers a long menu — realism , idealism , empiricism , materialism , constructivism , pragmatism , relativism , existentialism , and more. Each names something real. None settles the question, and a reader can spend a lifetime in that menu without ever eating.
Here is the definition this resource proceeds on:
"Truth is knowledge of things as they are, and as they were, and as they are to come." Doctrine and Covenants 93:24
Examine it on its own terms. It makes truth a matter of correspondence to actual states — past, present, and future. It is not a claim about God; it is a claim about what the word truth means. You may hold it without holding anything else here.
And notice what follows immediately. If truth spans what was , what is , and what is to come — and our natural faculties sample only a portion of that whole — then those faculties will reach a limit. Not because they are broken. Because of what they are.
1 How We Come to Know
The ceiling
Certain questions exceed the natural framework's reach:
Why is there something rather than nothing?
Does a loving God exist?
Does personal consciousness persist beyond death?
What is the ultimate purpose of my existence?
Science can describe how things work. It does not tell us why we are here — and it does not claim to.
This is not a failure. The framework itself predicts the limit.
Which leaves a genuine fork. You can accept permanent ignorance on the questions that matter most. Or you can ask whether there exists a faculty the four do not include.
Words of Plainness proposes a fifth: spiritual intuition — the direct perception of truth by inspiration or revelation. It is sometimes called irrational intuition. No insult is intended by that word; irrational here means only that human reasoning is not its source.
That is a claim, not a proof, and it is the claim everything downstream depends on. We will come back to how it can be tested.
Facilitator
Strongest objection, and worth surfacing yourself: is the ceiling real, or just the current edge of what we happen not to know yet?
Let that sit unresolved. The resource is stronger for it.
1 Reflection
Check your thinking
Which path establishes it?
"The Battle of Hastings took place in 1066." Which of the four natural paths is doing most of the work when you accept that?
A The senses
B Authority
C Reason
D Academic intuition
Authority. You did not witness it, cannot measure it, and cannot derive it. You accept it because historians say so — and you are right to. Notice how much of what you confidently "know" arrives this way. The question is never whether to trust authority but which authorities, and why.
Which of the four paths do you personally trust most — and has it ever failed you?
Is there a question your mind keeps returning to that reason alone has not settled?
Go deeper: Chapter 3, Academic Knowledge · Chapter 4, Spiritual Knowledge
2 Compelling Reasons to be a Theist
The reach toward contact — the theist claim in a single gesture.
"For since the creation of the world God's invisible qualities — his eternal power and divine nature — have been clearly seen, being understood from what has been made." Romans 1:20
Theism — from the Greek theos , "god." At its broadest, the belief that at least one deity exists; more restrictively, belief in God as Creator together with an openness to revelation. It contains an enormous range: deism, monotheism, trinitarianism, henotheism, pantheism, and more.
The Cosmological Argument. Whatever begins to exist has a cause. The universe began to exist. Therefore it has a cause — one which, being the cause of space and time, must be outside both. Aquinas, Summa Theologiae Ia, q. 2, a. 3; Leibniz; W.L. Craig, The Kalām Cosmological Argument , 1979.
The Teleological Argument. The ordered complexity of the universe — particularly the conditions required for life — is better explained by design than by chance. Paley, Natural Theology, 1802.
The Fine-Tuned Universe. Several physical constants fall within extraordinarily narrow life-permitting ranges. Alter the cosmological constant or the strong nuclear force slightly and there is no chemistry, no stars, no observers. Robin Collins, "The Teleological Argument: An Exploration of the Fine-Tuning of the Universe," in The Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology , 2009.
The Moral Argument. If objective moral obligations exist — if cruelty is genuinely wrong and not merely disfavored — they require a ground beyond human preference. Lewis, Mere Christianity I; Adams, Finite and Infinite Goods, 1999.
2 Compelling Reasons to be a Theist
The Argument from Contingency. Everything we observe might not have existed. A chain of contingent things, however long, does not explain itself. Leibniz; Swinburne, The Existence of God, 2nd ed. 2004.
Historicity. The resurrection is defended as a historical claim on the standard tools of ancient history: multiple early independent sources, the criterion of embarrassment, and the rise of a movement whose central claim was falsifiable in its own city within living memory. N.T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God, 2003.
Properly Basic Belief. Belief in God may be rational without being inferred — as belief in other minds, or in the reliability of memory, is rational without proof. Plantinga, Warranted Christian Belief, 2000.
Personal Experience. Enormous numbers of people across every culture and century report encounter with the divine — experiences they describe as more certain than argument and frequently transformative.
What theism must answer
The Problem of Evil. Gratuitous suffering — the child's cancer, the earthquake, the long private cruelty no one witnesses — is difficult to reconcile with a God simultaneously all-powerful, all-knowing, and wholly good. This is the strongest argument against the position I hold, and no answer I have encountered dissolves it entirely. Mackie, 1955; Rowe, 1979.
Divine Hiddenness. If God desires relationship with every person, the existence of sincere, non-resistant seekers who find nothing requires explanation. Schellenberg, 1993.
The Inference Gap. Even granting the cosmological and teleological arguments in full, they deliver a first cause and a designer. The distance to a God with a name, a character, and a Son is considerable — and is not crossed by argument.
Facilitator
Read the objections aloud yourself. A theist facilitator naming the problem of evil as unanswered buys enormous credibility.
Do not resolve it here. Section 7 addresses the shape of the answer, not the answer.
2 Reflection
Steel-man check
State it in one sentence
In your own words — not mine — what is the single strongest reason a thoughtful person becomes a theist?
Which of the three objections to theism do you find hardest to set aside?
If you are a theist, this is the exercise that keeps your position honest. If you are not, this is the exercise that keeps the conversation possible.
3 Compelling Reasons to be an Atheist
A definition, marked for examination — which is exactly how this section treats it.
"I had no need of that hypothesis." Pierre-Simon Laplace, reportedly, to Napoleon
Atheism — from a- and theos . Disbelief in, or denial of, the existence of divine beings. Atheism is not a belief system , and it is not the same as being irreligious. It is an active judgment, usually grounded in personal experience or philosophical argument, and there are many varieties of atheist.
The Burden of Proof. Extraordinary claims require proportionate evidence, and the burden falls on the one asserting. Bertrand Russell put it this way: if he claimed a china teapot were orbiting the sun somewhere between Earth and Mars, too small for any telescope to find, no one could disprove him — but nobody would think the claim deserved belief merely because it could not be refuted. Absent evidence, non-belief is the appropriate default, not a competing faith. Bertrand Russell, "Is There a God?", 1952; Sagan, 1995.
Sufficient Natural Explanation. Cosmology, evolutionary biology, and neuroscience account for the universe's origin, life's diversity, and the operations of mind without invoking an agent. Hume, Dialogues, 1779; Dennett, 1995.
The Problem of Evil, as positive argument. Not merely a difficulty for theism but evidence against it: gratuitous suffering is precisely what a universe without a benevolent governor would look like. Mackie, 1955; Rowe, 1979; Draper, 1989.
Religious Pluralism. Thousands of mutually exclusive traditions each claim revelation, and each is overwhelmingly predicted by the claimant's birthplace. Hume, "Of Miracles," Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding , 1748, sec. X.
3 Compelling Reasons to be an Atheist
Naturalistic Accounts of Belief. Cognitive science offers explanations for why humans reliably generate god-beliefs — agency detection, theory of mind, in-group cohesion — that require no god. Boyer, Religion Explained, 2001.
Textual and Historical Criticism. Sacred texts show every mark of human composition, redaction, and cultural situation.
Moral Autonomy. Ethics can be grounded in reason, empathy, and reciprocity without divine command — and the non-religious are not observably less ethical. Kant, Groundwork, 1785; Foot, Natural Goodness, 2001.
The Absence of Personal Experience. Where believers cite encounter as evidence, many have sought sincerely and found nothing. That absence is data too.
What atheism must answer
Grounding Objective Morality. If moral facts are real rather than preferred, naturalism must say what makes them so. If they are not real, "cruelty is wrong" reduces to "cruelty is disfavored" — and few atheists live as though that is all it means. Mackie conceded the difficulty, 1977.
The Brute-Fact Terminus. "Why is there something rather than nothing?" is answered with a stop rather than an explanation. That may be correct. It is not obviously more satisfying than the alternative stop.
Consciousness. Why physical processes are accompanied by subjective experience remains unexplained on any current account. Not an argument for God — a live limit on the claim that the natural story is complete. Chalmers, 1995.
3 Reflection
Steel-man check
State it in one sentence
In your own words, what is the single strongest reason a thoughtful person becomes an atheist?
If you are not an atheist: which of these arguments has the most force against your own position?
Facilitator
The highest-yield exercise in the whole resource: have each person argue the position they least hold, for two minutes.
Do it here, while all three are fresh.
4 Compelling Reasons to be Agnostic
Huxley's word was a method before it was a position — a way of looking, not a conclusion.
"Agnosticism, in fact, is not a creed, but a method… In matters of the intellect, follow your reason as far as it will take you, without regard to any other consideration… do not pretend that conclusions are certain which are not demonstrated or demonstrable." Thomas Henry Huxley, "Agnosticism," 1889
Agnosticism — coined by Huxley in 1869, by his own later account. Huxley's specific form is the hard one: ultimate truths of this kind are unknowable to any human, not merely unknown to the speaker. The soft form— I do not know, and I will not pretend to —is far more common, and most of the arguments below serve it just as well.
Inconclusive Evidence. The arguments on both sides are serious and neither is decisive. Suspending judgment where evidence is genuinely balanced is the correct response, not cowardice. Huxley, 1889; Clifford, 1877.
Limits of Human Cognition. Our concepts were built for mid-sized objects at moderate speeds. There is no reason to assume they scale to ultimate reality. Kant, Critique of Pure Reason, 1781; Nagel, 1974.
The Unknowable in Principle. The ultimate cause may be not merely undiscovered but permanently beyond the categories available to a finite mind. Spencer, First Principles, 1862.
Religious Pluralism. Committing to one tradition among thousands, all sincerely held, requires a confidence the evidence may not support.
Intellectual Humility. Declining to assert more than one has is a virtue, not an evasion.
What agnosticism must answer
The Practical Impossibility of Suspension. On this question you cannot actually abstain. You will live either as though your life is accountable to something beyond itself or as though it is not. Neutrality is available in theory and not in practice. Pascal, Pensées §233 (Brunschvicg) = §418 (Lafuma); James, "The Will to Believe," 1896.
Self-Application. "Ultimate truths are unknowable to any human" is itself a strong claim about ultimate truth. What grants access to that ?
Asymmetric Rigor. The evidential standard applied to religious claims is rarely the standard applied to history, other minds, or moral facts. Applied evenly, very little would survive.
4 Reflection
Steel-man check
Three positions, honestly weighed
In your own words, what is the strongest reason a thoughtful person remains agnostic?
Having now read all three argued fairly — has anything shifted? Even slightly?
What would change your mind? If nothing would, is your position responsive to evidence at all?
5 A Word for the Space Between
Look again at the horizontal axis
It offered you two options: you claim to know, or you hold that such things cannot be known. Gnostic or agnostic .
Thomas Henry Huxley coined agnostic in 1869 from the Greek — a- , "not," plus gnōstos , "known." It was an honest word and it filled a real gap. But it left another gap open, and that gap is where a great many thoughtful people actually live.
Paul named the condition long before Huxley named its denial. Writing to Corinth he said ek merous gar ginōskomen —
"For we know in part." 1 Corinthians 13:9
Not we do not know . Not we know fully . We know — really know — in part .
There has never been an English word for that. So I made one, on Huxley's own pattern: meros , "part," plus gnōstos , "known."
Merognostic. One who knows in part.
Enough pieces to see the picture. Honest about the ones still missing.
Illustration generated with ChatGPT to the author's specification, August 2026.
5 A Word for the Space Between
Set the four side by side
Gnostic (hard) Claims complete and certain knowledge.
Agnostic (hard) Claims that nothing can be known.
Skeptic Is not sure whether anything has been given.
Merognostic Holds what has genuinely been given, and declines to invent the rest.
On the map, that is the soft-gnostic half of the knowledge axis. I needed a word for it because "gnostic" alone is usually heard as the hard form, and "agnostic" gives away the part I actually hold.
Here is how I say it about myself:
I am a merognostic, not an agnostic. I know God is real. I know the Spirit has spoken to me. And I know, with the same honesty, that what I hold is a portion.
I offer the word; I do not assign it. It is a description of my own honesty, not a category for yours. If it names something you recognize, it is yours to use. If it does not, the grid is still perfectly good, and you are still perfectly welcome here.
One discipline keeps the word honest: it is a self-description of honest faith, never a box into which other souls may be sorted. The moment it becomes a tribe, it has betrayed the posture it names.
Go deeper: Merognosticism — A Plain Confession of Partial Knowing
Facilitator
This is the section that most often lands. Give it room and do not rush to the next slide.
Never say "so you're a merognostic." Let people claim it or leave it.
5 Reflection
Check your thinking
Which posture is speaking?
"I have felt God answer me. I could not tell you what heaven looks like, and I will not pretend to."
A Gnostic
B Agnostic
C Merognostic
D Skeptic
Merognostic. Two claims held at once: something real is known, and the knowing is admittedly partial. The agnostic would not say "I have felt God answer me." The gnostic would go on to describe heaven. This is the distinction most often collapsed — partial knowing gets mistaken for no knowing, and people conclude they have lost their faith when they have only grown honest about its edges.
Does this word name something you recognize — in yourself, or in someone you know?
6 The Third Axis
A question the grid raises and cannot answer
Two axes give four boxes. But something is obviously missing:
The grid says nothing about how a person lives.
A gnostic theist may be cruel. An agnostic atheist may be generous past all obligation. The map locates conviction and says nothing about consequence — and consequence is what anyone actually encounters when they meet you.
Before you advance
Propose a third axis
What would you measure? Justify it.
Facilitator
Collect two or three proposals aloud before advancing. Do not advance early — the reveal only works if they have committed first.
6 The Third Axis
What the machine proposed
In January 2025 I put this exact question to an AI — ChatGPT 4o Mini — and asked it to propose a z-axis for the exercise. It returned a spectrum of the consequences of actions, viewed through the framework of ecological ethics :
"When viewed through the lens of ecological ethics, the spectrum of good and evil is measured by the impact of beliefs and practices on both sustainability of community and quality of life." ChatGPT 4o Mini, 1 January 2025
The exercise in three dimensions. X: knowledge · Y: belief · Z: consequences of actions.
Working Definition GOOD results in interconnectedness, ethical stewardship, and holistic well-being.
GOOD creates stability within communities.
Working Definition EVIL results in disconnection, exploitation, and neglected quality of life.
EVIL destroys stability within communities.
One tree, two trajectories. The framework reads the ground, not the root.
6 The Third Axis
What I think of that answer
I want to say plainly why I kept this, because "an AI suggested it" is not a reason to keep anything.
I kept it because I taught it. For twenty-six years in a science laboratory I taught students to evaluate any system — a watershed, a cell, a food web, a population — by asking two questions: does it sustain itself over time, and does it sustain the things that depend on it? A system that consumes its own foundation is failing, however impressive its output looks in a given season. That is not a moral opinion. It is what the data does.
The machine, without being told any of that, reached for the same instrument.
What it gets right
It is measurable , or at least observable over time. It is available to everyone in the room — a committed atheist and a committed believer can both use it honestly without either conceding anything. And it lands on something scripture says constantly: by their fruits ye shall know them ( Matthew 7:20 ). The test of a thing is what it produces. That is an ecological claim before it is a theological one.
How to hold it
This diagram does not measure what happens to you, but how you respond to your existence. Loss, disaster, and temptation arrive from outside your lean; the axis reads only how you meet them. Read it at whatever scope you are examining—your own mind and body, a marriage, a business, your relationship with God—and read it on yourself. Pointed at a neighbor it only reads the wake he leaves, and reads it late.
Harm done in ignorance is still harm; the watershed does not ask what you meant. But evil on this axis is a lean, not an accident, and wisdom is largely the work of moving your accidental consequences into the column of things you chose.
Where it reads late
Two things stay upstream of everything this instrument knows how to measure. Another person's heart—which is why the axis is for self-location, not sorting. And your own turn. A life trending one direction can reverse, actually and not gradually, and the reversal is a change in what the person is before it is a change in anything the ground can show.
A good instrument pointed at the wrong depth. It measures the wake a life leaves behind. It cannot see the thing steering.
And notice—this is the same finding we reached about the natural framework in Section 1. A tool that works well within its domain, reaching a ceiling its own design predicts.
Facilitator
A promise creates a duty that outlasts the arithmetic. Ask the room whether the axis can see that.
6 Reflection
Check your thinking
Who can read the turn?
A man has spent a year quietly making amends for something no one knew he did. This month, none of it has produced a visible effect yet. What does the z-axis register?
A Nothing; it only reads consequences
B A strong negative; the original act still counts
C A strong positive, but only when he reads it himself
D His sincerity, accurately, to anyone who looks
C. The axis reads leaning, and he is the one person who can read his own. To everyone else it registers nothing yet, because no consequence has surfaced. That is the whole rule in one case: the instrument is for self-location, and it always reads other people late.
Where else in your life do you use a good instrument at the wrong depth?
Go deeper: Chapter 3 — "The Limitations of Academic Knowledge"
7 Reason and Revelation
Two halves of a whole
Rational and critical thinking are not evil. Yet scripture asks something that sounds frightening to the careful mind: "Trust in the Lord with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding" ( Proverbs 3:5-6 ).
The question is not whether to trust reason or to trust God. It is what each faculty is for .
Reason is not the enemy of faith, and scripture nowhere says it is. When Isaiah records the Lord's invitation — "Come now, and let us reason together" — the reasoning is not a concession God makes to skeptics. It is the form the invitation takes.
If any conflict exists between academic knowledge and spiritual knowledge, it is the result of a lack of sufficient information within one or both domains.
That is a strong claim, and it is meant to be. It says the appearance of conflict is a reliable signal that something is not yet known — not a verdict that one side must lose.
7 Reason and Revelation
Reason prepares the ground: it frames the question honestly, tests claims for coherence, guards against credulity, and interprets what revelation gives. Revelation answers what reason cannot reach, and hands reason new territory to work — because a revealed truth still has to be understood, integrated, and lived.
7 Reason and Revelation
How Peter came to know
"Lean not unto thine own understanding" is not an instruction to stop thinking. It is an instruction to stop asking one faculty to do work it was never built to do — and to stop concluding, when it fails, that the question has no answer.
Jesus asked Peter directly: "Whom say ye that I am?"
Peter answered, "Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God."
And Jesus told him where that knowledge had come from: "Flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven" ( Matthew 16:15-17 ).
Peter had walked with Him, watched Him, listened to Him — every natural faculty engaged and fully employed.
They brought him to the question. They did not produce the answer.
One honest difficulty remains, and it deserves to be named rather than managed. Spiritual knowledge cannot be transferred the way a proof can. No one can hand you their witness. This is not special pleading — the same is true of every genuinely first-person knowledge, and no one doubts the reality of grief or love on the grounds that neither can be demonstrated to a stranger. But it does mean the invitation must take a particular form.
It cannot be accept this . It can only be test this .
Two Halves of a Whole
An original song by Aaron Powner · Chapter 3 testimony
For truth is knowledge as things really are,
A light that shines on what is yet to come.
Science isn't blind and faith isn't lame
When we see them both as one.
The chorus inverts Einstein's line — "science without religion is lame, religion without science is blind" (Albert Einstein, "Science and Religion," 1941; reprinted in Ideas and Opinions , 1954).
▶ Listen & read full lyrics
7 Reflection
Reflect
The edge of your own knowing
Has reason ever brought you to a question it could not then answer? What did you do with it?
Chapter 3 claims apparent conflict always means missing information in one domain or the other. Is that too convenient?
Facilitator
The "too convenient" question is a fair challenge. Let it be pressed hard — the resource survives it better than a defensive answer would.
Bringing it together
Nobody has ever been argued into faith
If belief were installed by evidence, the strongest argument would produce the most believers, and it plainly does not. What actually forms conviction is a long accumulation: what you saw modeled, what you suffered, what you were given words for, what happened when you prayed and no one was watching.
The arguments matter — they clear obstacles and keep honest people honest — but they are not the mechanism. A constructed thing has to be built, and you have to do the building.
Which also means: your doubts are not disqualifying. They are part of the material. A faith assembled without them would be someone else's, borrowed and brittle.
One boundary, stated plainly
A belief must be livable — Christ said as much: "If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine" ( John 7:17 ). But usefulness is not truth. A belief can comfort, cohere, and produce good behavior and still be false.
Plainness is not pluralism.
I hold real humility about what mortals cannot know. No one living has surveyed heaven. But humility about the unrevealed is not relativism about the revealed. A belief should be adaptable in the sense that you keep growing into it — seeing further, understanding better, repenting where you were wrong. That is not the same as the belief itself bending to accommodate you. The first is discipleship. The second is preference wearing better clothes.
Bringing it together
Place yourself again
You located yourself before we began. Seven sections later, place yourself again — honestly. Movement is not the goal, and staying exactly where you were is a legitimate result. The point is to notice.
This map does not measure what happens to you. It measures your present state, your intentions, and your leanings.
Click to place yourself now. The vertical axis is degree of belief—what you hold to be true. The horizontal axis is knowledge—the degree to which you claim to know it, and can give warrant for the claim.
Full definitions and the caveat are on the opening grid.
What accounts for that — the movement, or the staying put?
Where to go from here
Two honest next steps
Everything to this point has been reasoning. What follows is not — and you may take either path, or neither, and remain entirely welcome.
1 · Run the experiment
Test the claim rather than accept it. Set a commitment, a start date, and a date to evaluate honestly. Roughly thirty days.
2 · Read the long version
Everything compressed here is developed at length in the first six chapters of Words of Plainness — the search for meaning, academic knowledge, spiritual knowledge, sincere prayer, and faith in Jesus Christ.
The experiment
Just as the natural faculties allow beliefs to be tested by observation and application, spiritual knowledge allows for a kind of sacred experiment that produces observable outcomes. Three scripture verses summarize this, escalating in what they ask and what they promise:
"If any man will do his will, he shall know of the doctrine, whether it be of God." John 7:17 — a conditional claim with a predicted result. Not feel better . Know.
"He that hath my commandments, and keepeth them… I will love him, and will manifest myself to him." John 14:21 — the deeper promise
"Even if ye can no more than desire to believe, let this desire work in you." Alma 32:27 — the honest entry point. You do not need conviction to begin.
Record your commitment
Part A: Put it into practice and see for yourself
Thirty days is a good length. There are two honest ways to run it — either one is a real experiment:
1 · Practice something new Pick one to three commandments of Christ and keep them deliberately for the period you set.
2 · Examine something you already do Pick one to three behaviors you already practice, and observe honestly how they affect you and the people around you — measured on the ecological scale of good and evil from Section 6.
What will you do? Name the commandment or behavior specifically. If you need help choosing, open the Keep My Commandments ↗ web app and browse until you find a few that are to your liking.
Start date
Date you will stop and evaluate honestly
Decide now, before you begin: what would you accept as a result? What would you not be entitled to conclude either way?
Record your prayer
Part B: Prepare, seek revelation, and reflect
Keeping the commandments you chose in Part A is preparation for this. At any point during your thirty days, and as often as you need to, take what you are learning to God in prayer. This kind of prayer is discussed in greater depth in my writings, Chapter 4: Spiritual Knowledge .
"You can learn to reach outside of yourself with your mind and heart, praying with sincerity to perceive truth spiritually. Ask if God is really there. There is no need for memorized phrases or complicated communication. Just speak what is in your mind and heart. He will listen."
How will you prepare yourself for this prayer, what will you ask, and what did you notice afterward?
About Keep My Commandments — a daily discipleship tracker. Choose a commandment, mark the days, and keep your own record of what happens. If you would rather see what it is before opening it, read about it here .
The long version
Chapter 1 · Introduction — why plainness, and who this is for.
Chapter 2 · Our Search — the questions that motivate any honest search for meaning.
Chapter 3 · Academic Knowledge — the four paths, the nature of truth, and the ceiling of the natural framework. Section 1 of this resource is a compression of this chapter.
Chapter 4 · Spiritual Knowledge — the fifth faculty: how revelation is received and what it feels like.
Chapter 5 · Sincere Prayer — the practical how-to for Part B of the experiment.
Chapter 6 · Embrace the Savior — where the whole search has been going.
Open Movement 1 — Chapters 1–6 → Start reading at Chapter 1 →
Facilitator
Do not press for a choice in a group setting. Name both paths, then stop talking.
The most powerful close is the last line on the next slide. Read it and let the silence hold.
Close
What you take with you
You came in somewhere on the map. You have now seen your own position argued at its strongest, and the two you do not hold argued the same way. You have seen a framework reach its ceiling, and a word offered for the honest space between claiming everything and claiming nothing.
None of that requires you to change. It only asks that whatever you hold, you hold it knowingly — and that you not mistake the edge of one faculty for the edge of what is real.
"Come now, and let us reason together, saith the Lord." Isaiah 1:18
You are welcome here whatever you decide. That was true before you started and it is true now.
Your record
Take your reflections with you
Everything you wrote is saved only in this browser. Nothing was sent anywhere and no one has seen it. Download it, print it, or keep it here for next time.

pages.title: Introduction
pages.text:
Chapter 1: Introduction
The Human Condition
We are all so very human. Our wandering feet carry us along many curious and often frightening paths. Our untamed hearts pull or push us in unexpected directions. Our wide eyes marvel at the fleeting scenes of beauty and filth which unfold around us. Our grasping hands shape the environments and cultures we touch. Our unceasing voices speak much, yet too often say little. Our twitching ears are filled with the discordant noises of life. Our restless minds wrestle with the meaning of it all, desperate to forget the bitter and remember the sweet. Yet humanity occasionally manages to find itself, to gentle itself—to see, free, quiet, harmonize, and understand itself.
The writers of this book are brothers. We use the word writers because we feel that we are not the authors of any particular words of greatness. Instead, we are hunters and gatherers of knowledge. We till and seed the soils of our souls hoping to harvest wisdom.
We are native citizens of the world, yet we perceive the foreign nature of mankind's walk upon the Earth. Though our journey is not complete, my brother and I have found ourselves both on the side of right and clearly in the wrong often enough to have gained an abiding appreciation for the many profound lessons that can be gleaned from the human experience.
Origin of Our Writings
As a young man I, Aaron, chose to serve a mission to the people of Argentina for The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. In my idealism, I hoped to bring light and goodness to people who had been less fortunate. I like to believe that I left something of value behind for the people I came to love, but I returned deeply transformed by my experiences.
The new thoughts I learned to think and the tender feelings I came to cherish during my mission planted in my heart a seed of passion for sharing things of worth with others. I returned to a world that is far more complex and fast-paced than my mission experience had been, and I found it somehow the lesser for it. In spite of this, that latent kernel of desire swelled in my heart and grew. I began searching for ideas, experiences, and things of great worth. I wrote of them. I did not know to whom I was writing. I had not considered my audience.
After some time, I suspected that I might be crafting letters to my unborn children. I came to believe that my collection of writings could become a simple legacy that I might leave behind at my journey's end. I became convinced that stories of my life, my tempering experiences, and meaningful traditions, along with my humble understandings, precious beliefs, and faith-filled encouragement are the only meaningful inheritance I can bequeath to my posterity.
When my adventures with family and children began, my yearning to gather and then write of these things became a driving need. In my late thirties, I felt a strong urge to better organize my hard-learned lessons and happy discoveries in the form of a book or collection of letters. I am not finished learning, but I felt my experience and understanding was sufficient to truly begin sharing. Spending a few hours each night, as I could spare, I finished my first rough draft in a little more than six months.
I shared my collected works with my older brother, Jim. He has long been more than an example of manhood to me; he is a trusted friend. His comments, questions, suggestions, and assistance became such an important part of editing my letters that I realized they are as much the result of his life experiences as they are of my own.
Our long studies and preparations seemed to take on a life of their own. We quickly adopted the belief that such beautiful ideas and experiences must be shared in words of plainness. This philosophy became the title of our work. We understand that the publication of such personal things may open us to criticism and unforeseen consequences. We have long considered and earnestly prayed about our decision to act in accordance with our desires. We offer our Words of Plainness to you with hope, for they are the treasured things of our souls.
Relevance of Our Writings
The topics of our writings seem appropriate for our day and age. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints and its members have become the subject of a surprising amount of social media coverage, both favorable and not. Debate over the Church's history, beliefs, and practices appears in popular tabloids, newspapers, books, television programs, online forums, and even in widely public political arenas.
Since the 1830s, newspapers and publications of detractors have called us "Mormons" or refer to our theology as "Mormonism" because we use the Book of Mormon as a companion to the Bible as a source of scripture about the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Over the generations the term became culturally widespread. Some members of the Church even adopted the term "Mormon" to rob it of its derogatory intent towards our culture and beliefs. Why have recent Church leaders discouraged the use of the term? Why don't members prefer the term? Simply put, we aren't followers of Mormon. Along the same line of thinking, we don't worship Joseph Smith, and we don't replace the Bible with the Book of Mormon either.
With regards to faith and religion, it seems like common sense that if you want to know what a Baptist believes you should ask a Baptist. If you want to know what a Methodist believes you should ask a Methodist. This is also true for Roman Catholics, Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims, and so on. It is equally true that not all Baptists believe the same body of doctrines or behave the same way. Likewise are the Methodists, Catholics, Buddhists, Hindus, Muslims, and so forth.
In recent years, leaders of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints have discouraged using the name "Mormon" to refer to the Church or its members. This is because it obscures the Church's Christ-centered identity and reduces a complex, Christ-centered faith to a nickname given by those who first coined it in derision.
Instead, Church officials have emphasized using the full name of the Church or "The Church of Jesus Christ" for brevity. Also, the term "Latter-day Saints" is preferred for referring to its members. This reflects theological accuracy, historical continuity, and respect for religious self-identification. Using precise language not only honors the beliefs of its members but also avoids reinforcing misunderstandings about their faith, practices, and relationship to broader Christianity. Our goal is to keep the focus of worship squarely on Jesus Christ, where it belongs.
In modern times, the human right to self-identification for cultures and individuals has become an important topic within national and international legal systems. More importantly, it is a matter of civility and correct social skills. Latter-day Saints reserve the same right as other groups and individuals to self-identify and invite the respectful use of the name and identity we embrace.
Are We Christians?
Many outsiders claim Latter-day Saints are not Christians. Some declare that we believe in the wrong Jesus. Do we worship a different Jesus? Do we teach a different gospel from other Christians?
Simply: the name of our church is The Church of Jesus Christ.
Specifically: Latter-day Saints follow Jesus of Nazareth, whom many religions embrace as the Christ, the promised Messiah, and the divine Son of God. To become members, we embrace the truth that we are all sinners, having fallen short of the glory of God. We accept that we need God's forgiveness. We have faith that Jesus of Nazareth is the Christ, that He died on the cross for our sins and rose from the dead. We take His name upon us, make sincere covenants through baptism and receiving the Gift of the Holy Ghost. We labor to continue to turn from our sins, inviting God into our hearts and lives. We trust Jesus as our Savior and follow Him as our Lord.
Strangely: An enormous volume of misinformation and malicious propaganda exists about the restored gospel of Jesus Christ and members of our Church. Importantly, the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints does not claim that the Church as an institution or its mortal leaders are infallible or free from error.
During our long years as public school teachers, we struggled to convince students of the vital importance of using authoritative sources of information that have been developed from multiple perspectives when doing research and in the formation of lasting opinions. Gossip columns, hate blogs, and literature critical of the Church are tantalizing reads, but they seldom offer much in the way of actual credibility. Tracing the citations and sources of such information, one finds little more than hearsay and quotations either taken out of context or hastily borrowed from other unverifiable sources. Though false information might be presented energetically and even well-received by many, it remains fundamentally untrue.
Throughout history, it has been consistently true that the odd combination of ignorance and confidence eventually leads to suffering, oppression, bigotry, and hatred. We believe that it is essential to the character of each human being to search for truth, meaning, and lasting happiness—and that we must do so while upholding the virtues of honesty, compassion, and tolerance. Surely these are the noblest of emerging characteristics possessed by enlightened individuals and found within civilized cultures.
It is surely anti-Christian to bash, belittle, and discourage anyone's faith in Jesus Christ. No one has perfect knowledge of all truth, and all believers seek to follow Christ as best we can. Jesus said, "whoever is not against us is for us." Also, Christ condemned the Pharisee's spirit—certain, superior, quick to condemn. It poses a danger in every age, and none of us is immune to it. We must not claim to know more about what others believe than they do.
Accordingly, we claim the right to be the supreme mortal authorities over what we personally believe, how this makes us feel, and how we interpret the effects of living as Latter-day Saints within our own life experiences.
What We Hold in Common With Other Christians
Our Articles of Interfaith Discipleship declare, in full, what beliefs we hold in common with all who confess Jesus Christ. In brief, this is the gospel they proclaim:
What we trust for salvation
God is the Eternal Father—loving, good, and sustaining—known truly only as far as He reveals Himself.
Jesus Christ is the promised Messiah, Divinity made flesh, the living image of the Father's heart: sinless, crucified for our sins, risen on the third day, and the living measure of every witness.
Salvation comes through Christ's grace and Atonement—saving us from sin and death and forming His image in us, from creation in His image to fellowship with Him as co-heirs.
We do not reduce salvation to any single part. It is the whole work of Christ held together—grace and Atonement; faith, repentance, and the new birth; the Christlike virtues; and the Spirit's sanctifying, sealing work unto eternal life.
The Kingdom is at hand. Eternal life is to know God and walk in fellowship with His Son, begun the moment we come to Him—not a reward withheld until death or perfection.
The grave is not the end. Christ's resurrection is both the promise and the proof; every soul will rise and stand honestly before a merciful God, and what is entrusted to Him is not lost.
Christ is enough—for the flawed, the weary, the wounded, and the searching, in every tribe and tongue and tradition. No soul is barred from Him for want of a perfect understanding.
How we follow as disciples
We walk humbly, knowing in part—receiving gladly what God reveals plainly, leaving the secret things to Him, and binding no one's conscience with speculation.
We search the scriptures by the Spirit, worshiping God alone and never idolizing the vessel through whom His word comes.
We take Christ as our fixed point—the North Star—with the Spirit as our compass and scripture as our map, each calibrated always to Him.
We become disciples by covenant: surrendering our will into His, taking up the cross daily, repenting when we fall short, and living the gospel rather than merely professing it.
We live by God's grace as a transformative power, not a license to sin. Discipleship is a walk, a journey, a maturing, a becoming—doing good whether or not it is seen or rewarded.
We receive every soul who comes to Christ as family, refusing to weaponize doctrine or defend the walls He never built.
We deal gently with the weak and the searching, leave judgment to the one righteous Judge, and never stand between the Shepherd and His lambs.
For more detailed information, read the full Articles of Interfaith Discipleship .
Our Credentials as Latter-day Saints
My brother and I have spent our lives within the culture and practices of the faith of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. We are active members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, yet we feel the need to offer some few credentials which establish our general worthiness to represent regular, ordinary, everyday members of our Church and that we live a reasonably common Latter-day Saint lifestyle.
Our Conversion and Upbringing
We were born to Lutheran parents. Our mother investigated and eventually chose to convert to The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Many friends and relatives questioned or even opposed her decision. She was baptized while she was pregnant with Aaron, the younger of the two writer brothers. James also later converted. Our childhoods were strongly enmeshed in the culture and society of Church members. We actively and regularly attended worship services and participated in the Church's Primary and youth programs.
Priesthood and Service
We were both formally ordained to the "Lesser" Priesthood in our adolescence. We were successively set apart in the offices of Deacon, Teacher, and Priest. We feel that we faithfully officiated in these offices by preparing and passing the emblems of the Lord's Supper, collecting fast offerings for the poor, home teaching our fellow members, baptizing those who came into the Church, and assisting in assorted temporal responsibilities.
As young adults we were both ordained to the "Higher" Priesthood. We were both set apart as Elders and performed as such. We were both called and set apart to full-time proselyting missionary service. We both received our temple endowments, whereby we made sacred covenants (promises) with God in His holy temple.
We have been married to our wives in the Temple of the Lord. We have done our best to raise our children to walk uprightly before the Lord. We have been called and set apart in many positions of service throughout our lives in the Church. Currently, James is serving as a High Priest in his ward. Aaron is serving as an Elder in his ward. We anticipate, God willing, a lifetime of service to our fellow members and to all God's children.
Our Lives as Latter-day Saints
We worship with our congregations. We fast and we pray. We read and study the Scriptures. We have paid tithes and given offerings. We have attended and officiated in temple worship. We are not perfect, but we continually repent and seek to align our lives with God's will. We strive to cultivate the fruits of the Spirit: patience, kindness, love, charity, peace, joy, meekness, etc. We seek to obtain the gifts of the Spirit described in 1 Corinthians 12 : wisdom, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, speaking in tongues, and interpretation of tongues. We study with open hearts and minds.
We seek to be of service to our fellowman. We seek to be forgiving, slow to anger, and to avoid unrighteous behaviors. We seek to be good neighbors. We seek to be good friends and good examples, even if no one is watching. We seek to be humble and teachable. We seek to be genuine disciples of Jesus Christ. We bear public witness that Jesus Christ lives, that He loves us, that He has made it possible for us to be forgiven of our sins, and that all are invited to come unto Him and be sanctified of their sins and made righteous if they will but have faith in Him, repent, be baptized, and follow Him to the end of their mortal journey.
Christ-Centered Plainness
Our witness of Jesus Christ is the most important aspect of Words of Plainness. We do not question or deny anyone else's status as Christians. Regardless of the opinions of critics, members of our Church are Christians. We are of the same Spirit as other Christians, though of a different understanding. We believe the words of the Apostle Paul: "No man can say that Jesus is the Lord, but by the Holy Ghost." Again, in the truest sense of the word "Christian," theological and doctrinal differences between religious denominations need not determine whether a person is a sincere disciple of Christ. Words of Plainness is an attempt to explain what it means to be a sincere disciple for any Christ-believer.
Though we authors are imperfect and subject to the same temptations and foolishness as are all members of humankind, we labor to invite the Spirit of God to sanctify our lives—to become holy through the grace of Christ through continued repentance and devotion to the gospel of Jesus Christ. We invite others to do the same out of genuine concern and love for all God's children. We hope to truly be worthy of the title "Saints" in these latter days.
Kinship with All Believers
We as Latter-day Saints happily recognize the light and goodness found in all people who search for truth, meaning, and lasting happiness. We feel a close kinship with all those who believe in Jesus Christ. We do not discourage their faith. Faithful Latter-day Saints who understand the core teachings of the restored gospel do not condemn others; rather, we humbly believe that Jesus Christ is the Savior of us all. If you cannot agree with the doctrines of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, we plead with you at least to believe in Christ. If we all heed the Savior's call, "Come follow me," we will undoubtedly find ourselves together in His kingdom at last.
We truly believe that all Christians have more in common than what divides us. However, if any of us dare to persecute one another over differences in doctrine and silly rumors—as though we were truly wise in any way—we will undoubtedly find ourselves both unworthy and uncomfortable upon leaving this life to stand in judgment before God. Jesus said that those who are angry with a brother without cause are in danger of judgment. Further, Jesus "came not to condemn the world." Do we, then, have any right to condemn one another? Are any of us better or wiser than He?
When Latter-day Saints invite others to investigate the Church, we do not attempt to take away what light and faith they have. Rather, we invite all to come and see what the Lord has done in our lives in the hope that we can add to the light others already possess. A vital point to make is that those who think that Latter-day Saints believe only members of our Church will reach heaven misunderstand our doctrine of God's expansive mercy and multiple degrees of glory.
When Faith Is Tried
Some who come to these writings arrive with a settled faith. Others arrive in the middle of a hard season—when the faith they were given no longer fits the questions they have come to ask, and they cannot tell whether what is shaking is their belief in God or only the frame that once held it. If that is where you stand, we want to say it plainly: doubt is not the same as departure, and the loss of an old certainty is not the loss of Christ. The treasure and the vessel that carries it are not the same thing. A vessel may crack without the treasure being spilled.
We know this road because we have walked it. We had to learn, slowly and sometimes painfully, to tell the difference between the gospel of Jesus Christ and the culture that had grown up around it—the inherited assumptions, the borrowed certainties, the things people had added to what God actually said. We do not say this to fault the faith that raised us; we say it because every vessel that carries the treasure is an earthen one, ours included. What we found, when we stopped clutching the frame and reached instead for Christ, was not less faith but more—and a deeper respect for sincere believers whose path looks nothing like our own. The work can be frightening, for the one who walks it and for those who love them. Walk it anyway. Surrender to Christ, seek the best gifts, and trust that the God who began the work is faithful to finish it.
And to those who remain settled while someone they love begins to wander: we know that you worry, and that the worry is love. But hear the consolation before you let the fear harden. The Shepherd does not forget the one sheep that strays; He leaves the ninety and nine and goes after it until He finds it, for it is not the will of your Father which is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish. His reach is longer than your arms, and longer than the grave—He has other sheep that are not of this fold, and He remembers even those who never knew His name. You may trust Him with the ones you cannot reach.
And because you may trust Him with them, you are freed—from the burden, and the danger, of appointing yourself their judge. Guard your own heart here, for the measure you give will be the measure you receive. Do not let grief curdle into indignation, or let love for the truth become a club; the Good Physician does not break the bruised reed nor quench the smoking flax, and neither must we. This is not indifference to truth—error is still error, and we are called to restore the wandering gently, watching our own hearts lest we also be tempted. The honest question, when another's faith falters, is never only "What is wrong with them?" but also, quietly, "Lord, is it I?"
Underneath all of it is one plain truth: we know in part, and He knows in full. We cannot see the end of anyone's story; He can, and He loves them more than we do. That single humility is enough to keep the doubter walking and to keep the faithful from the wrong spirit. We have written more fully about these things elsewhere—about partial knowing , about the treasure in broken vessels , about the long reach of Christ toward those who wander , and the lament of the God who would gather them —and those pathways will be waiting whenever you are ready for them.
Finding Your Way Through Our Writings
These writings have grown into something larger than a single book. They live here as a study you can move through at your own pace, gathered into two volumes—and everything in them is meant to lead you toward the same Person.
Volume 1 of our writings is for everyone who will consider Jesus Christ. It begins with the foundations of faith, moves through the life and character of the Savior, and arrives at the practices that shape anyone who follows Him. It asks no prior beliefs of you and presses no membership upon you—only a willing heart. Whatever your tradition, or if you carry none at all, this volume is meant to meet you where you stand.
Volume 2 of our writings is for those whom the Spirit moves to go further. Here we open the fullness of what Latter-day Saints believe—the covenants, the nature of God, the Plan of Salvation, and the hope of our eternal inheritance. We have placed it second on purpose. We would rather you meet Christ with us first, on the ground we already share, than ask you to weigh our distinctive claims before that friendship has had time to form. This is not concealment; it is the order in which we ourselves came to understand, and the order in which we believe these things are best received.
And these pages are more than words to read. You can listen as well as read, pause to reflect or to record your own witness, and follow the deeper study pathways and companion essays wherever a question opens beneath your feet. The Writings page will always be your map: it shows you where to begin and what has newly arrived, so you need never wonder what comes next.
Our Plea to You
Our work has been to gather plain and precious truths that God has revealed concerning His personal nature and His will for mankind. We generally write in our own words and according to our own understanding, but we cite the sources of truth. We draw from the inspired teachings of prophets and apostles of God, both ancient and modern. We quote holy scripture—the Bible, the Book of Mormon, the Doctrine and Covenants, and the Pearl of Great Price—which contain the word of God. We encourage you to study the references from which we have drawn in performing this labor of love.
We plead with you not to be offended by the fact that we may hold some ideas different from your own. More importantly, we implore you not to rebel against the idea that there is a higher authority than mankind, or against the idea that we all ought to obey commandments of God. We encourage you not to reject the idea that mankind needs to be saved. At the very least, we need to be saved from sources of unhappiness: ignorance of life's purpose, the consequences of wandering from wisdom's path, and our estrangement from our Creator.
My brother and I take great joy and comfort in what small light and knowledge God has given to us. We feel as if we have awakened from a deep sleep, made new and somehow more whole by our acquaintance with God and His Son. We openly confess our own imperfections and limitations. We do not seek to set ourselves up as a source of light for the world. Rather, we seek to remind all humanity that God is the light by which all may see in the dark.
What you get out of reading our Words of Plainness depends entirely upon what you are looking for as you study them. We hope that you find in our writings encouragement and inspiration to believe in God and in His Son Jesus Christ. Our prayer is that you will be blessed by the Spirit and grace of God as you consider our words, in the name of Jesus Christ. Amen.
