pages.title: Conversation Builder — Seeking Jesus of Nazareth
pages.text:
SCN-L01 · Latter-day Saint learner
"You believe in a different God"
I don't think Latter-day Saints are Christian. You believe in a different God. A Baptist friend
What is really being asked
Whether the God you worship is the God of the Bible — and whether the differences are total or located.
Where the map answers it
A Father
A Son
A Savior
D Incorporeal / without body
D Without parts / simple
G GOD-01
G GOD-03
+ The Father is an embodied, tangible, glorified person; humanity is made in His image.
Resolves to
Here we genuinely agree.
Here we directly disagree.
Here one tradition makes an additional claim.
A response you could give
I understand why it feels that way, so let me be exact rather than defensive. We worship the Father of Jesus Christ; we confess Jesus as the Son of God, Lord, and only Savior; we believe the Holy Spirit gives life. On those the creeds and our scriptures say the same thing. Where we really do disagree is the nature of God's being: your confession says God is without body or parts, and we believe the Father has a glorified body and that the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are three persons one in purpose. That's a real difference, and I won't minimize it. But it's a difference about how God exists, not about which God we love and pray to.
Avoid. Do not say "we believe the same things" — the divergence on divine embodiment is direct and your friend knows it. Do not answer a question about God with a testimony of the Church.
Sources on this card: Articles of Faith 1:1 · D&C 130:22 · D&C 20:21
SCN-L02 · Latter-day Saint learner
"Same words, different meanings"
We use a lot of the same words, but I think we mean different things by them. A Catholic neighbor
What is really being asked
Whether shared vocabulary is hiding disagreement — and whether you'll be honest about where it does.
Where the map answers it
Q Creator / Maker
Q Spirit
Q Immutable / unchangeable
A Merciful
Resolves to
Here we genuinely agree.
Here we share a concern but mean it differently.
A response you could give
You're right, and I'd rather find those places than paper over them. Take 'Creator.' We both confess God as Maker of heaven and earth, and we mean it. But your tradition teaches creation from nothing, and ours teaches that God organized eternal elements — so the word is shared and the picture behind it isn't. Same with 'Spirit': we both say God is spirit; we also believe spirit is refined matter. On the other hand, when we say God is merciful, or just, or holy, I don't think there's a hidden difference at all. So the honest answer is: some words we share all the way down, some we share at the surface. Want to go through a few?
Avoid. Do not concede that every shared word is hollow; most of the positive language about God's character is shared in the same sense.
Sources on this card: Abraham 3:24 · D&C 131:7-8 · Mormon 9:19
SCN-L03 · Latter-day Saint learner
"If you have revelation, why talk about shared truth?"
If you believe God restored the truth through Joseph Smith, why do you keep saying you share our faith? Either the churches lost it or they didn't. An evangelical acquaintance
What is really being asked
Whether 'restoration' means the rest of Christianity was wrong about everything.
Where the map answers it
A Living
A Love / loving
A Judge
+ Human beings possessed personal premortal existence.
+ Human beings may receive divine fulness and become like God, canonically described as becoming gods.
Resolves to
Here we genuinely agree.
Here one tradition makes an additional claim.
A response you could give
Restoration doesn't mean replacement. When I read the Nicene Creed, most of what it says about God — living, true, almighty, Father, Son, Lord, judge, giver of life — I believe exactly as written. What we believe was restored is priesthood authority, ordinances, and some teachings the creeds don't contain: that we lived with God before birth, that families can be eternal, that we can become like Him. Those are additions relative to the creeds, and I hold them as revealed. But they don't erase what Christians have always taught about God's character. I'd put it this way: much is shared, some is understood differently, a few things we directly disagree on, and some things we add. All four are true at once.
Avoid. Do not say the creeds are 'an abomination' as a conversation opener; the app teaches the map, not the polemic. Do not imply other Christians lack the Spirit.
Sources on this card: Abraham 3:22-23 · D&C 132:19-20 · D&C 20:17-19
SCN-L04 · Latter-day Saint learner
"Theosis is not exaltation"
You say we both teach that people become like God. But theosis is nothing like your exaltation. An Orthodox friend
What is really being asked
Whether you are borrowing an Orthodox word to make a Latter-day Saint doctrine sound ancient.
Where the map answers it
+ Human beings may receive divine fulness and become like God, canonically described as becoming gods.
D Greater dissimilarity than similarity
Q No adequate likeness or comparison
Resolves to
Here we share a concern but mean it differently.
Here we directly disagree.
Here one tradition makes an additional claim.
A response you could give
That's fair, and I want to respect the difference. Your tradition teaches that people share in God's life — His energies — without ever sharing His essence; the gap between Creator and creature stays infinite. We teach that we are literally God's spirit children and can receive His fulness. So the shared part is real: both of us believe salvation is more than forgiveness — it's being transformed into the likeness of Christ. The difference is also real: you'd say the likeness never becomes kinship, and we'd say it already is kinship. I'd rather say that plainly than claim the Fathers taught what we teach.
Avoid. Do not claim Irenaeus or Athanasius taught Latter-day Saint exaltation. The paper codes theosis as an antecedent, not an equivalent.
Sources on this card: D&C 76:58 · Romans 8:16-17 · Moses 1:39
SCN-L05 · Latter-day Saint learner
"Unity means they'll agree with us"
Unity of faith just means that eventually everyone will come around to what we believe. A fellow ward member
What is really being asked
Whether 'one faith' (Ephesians 4:5) requires uniformity of doctrine now — and how to treat Christians who never join.
Where the map answers it
A Holy
A Love / loving
A Savior
Resolves to
Here we genuinely agree.
A response you could give
I used to think that too. But look at what we already share with the Baptist family down the street: they worship the same Father, trust the same Savior, and try to keep His commandments. That's not nothing — it's most of what the creeds say about God. Unity of faith can mean shared devotion and common discipleship without pretending we agree on everything, and it can mean respecting their conscience the way we want ours respected. Our job is to know what we believe clearly, name the differences honestly, and love them either way. If the Spirit brings them further, wonderful. If not, they are still Christ's.
Avoid. Do not turn 'unity' into 'everyone must think like me.' Do not treat other Christians as projects rather than neighbors.
Sources on this card: Ephesians 4:5 · John 17:21 · Articles of Faith 1:11
SCN-C01 · Learner from another Christian tradition
"Don't bother — it's a cult"
Why would you learn what Mormons believe? It's a cult. Just tell them about Jesus. A friend at church
What is really being asked
Whether understanding a tradition before speaking to it is a compromise — and what Latter-day Saints actually confess about Jesus.
Where the map answers it
A Son
A Lord
A Savior
D Incorporeal / without body
Resolves to
Here we genuinely agree.
Here we directly disagree.
A response you could give
I do want to tell them about Jesus — which is exactly why I want to know what they already believe about Him. Their scriptures call Him the Only Begotten Son, Lord, and Savior; they pray to the Father in His name; they'd affirm nearly everything our confession says about God's holiness, mercy, and justice. Where we really part ways is the nature of God — they believe the Father has a body, we confess He is spirit without body or parts — and on what salvation finally includes. If I lead with 'cult,' I'll never get to those real differences, and I'll be arguing against beliefs they don't hold. Understanding first isn't compromise; it's how you speak the truth in love.
Avoid. Do not repeat claims the sources don't support (e.g., that Latter-day Saints worship Joseph Smith or deny Christ's divinity).
Sources on this card: Ephesians 4:15 · 1 Peter 3:15
SCN-C02 · Learner from another Christian tradition
"We're Christians just like you"
We believe in Jesus too. We're Christians just like you. A Latter-day Saint coworker
What is really being asked
Whether you will grant what is shared without pretending the rest is the same — and whether you can say so kindly.
Where the map answers it
A Son
A Savior
D Incorporeal / without body
D Without parts / simple
G GOD-02
Resolves to
Here we genuinely agree.
Here we directly disagree.
A response you could give
I believe you believe in Jesus — that's clear from how you talk about Him, and I don't doubt your devotion. I'd honestly say we share a lot: one Father, Jesus as Son of God and Savior, the Holy Spirit, a real call to holiness. Where I think we're different — and I'd rather say it than have it sitting between us — is about who God is in His being. My church confesses one God in three persons of one substance, without body or parts. Yours teaches that the Father has a body and that the three are separate beings. That's not a small thing to me. So 'just like you' isn't quite right, but neither is 'nothing like you.' Can we talk about the real differences?
Avoid. Do not use 'not Christian' as a conversation-ender; name the specific divergence instead.
Sources on this card: Nicene Creed · Westminster Confession II.1
SCN-C03 · Learner from another Christian tradition
"God has a body"
The Bible says we're made in God's image. God has a body of flesh and bone — Joseph Smith saw Him. A Latter-day Saint friend
What is really being asked
How to respond to the single largest divergence without caricature — and where the scriptures each side cites actually sit.
Where the map answers it
D Invisible
D Incorporeal / without body
D Without parts / simple
D Without passions / impassible
+ The Father is an embodied, tangible, glorified person; humanity is made in His image.
Resolves to
Here we directly disagree.
Here we share a concern but mean it differently.
A response you could give
This is the place I think we most disagree, so let me be careful. When Paul calls God 'invisible' and Jesus says 'God is a Spirit,' my tradition takes that as describing what God is — without body, parts, or passions. You read those as describing what mortals can perceive, not what God is. So we're reading the same verses and reaching different conclusions about God's nature; that's a direct disagreement, not a misunderstanding. What I'd add is that your view isn't random — it flows from believing we are literally God's children in His image. I don't share the conclusion, but I understand the reasoning, and I'd rather argue with the real thing than a cartoon of it.
Avoid. Do not say Latter-day Saints think God is 'just a man'; their sources say glorified, exalted, and perfect. Do not claim 1 Timothy 1:17 settles the question for them — the scope of 'invisible' is exactly what's disputed.
Sources on this card: 1 Timothy 1:17 · John 4:24 · Thirty-Nine Articles I
SCN-C04 · Learner from another Christian tradition
"Saved by grace, after all we can do"
We believe we're saved by grace — after all we can do. A Latter-day Saint friend
What is really being asked
Whether Latter-day Saints teach salvation by works — and what 'saved' means in their vocabulary.
Where the map answers it
A Gracious
A Savior
+ Human beings may receive divine fulness and become like God, canonically described as becoming gods.
C ICC-002
Resolves to
Here we genuinely agree.
Here we share a concern but mean it differently.
A response you could give
I'll admit that phrase used to sound to me like 'grace fills in whatever you couldn't earn.' Then I read what your own leaders say about it — that no one can earn heaven, that salvation can't be bought with obedience — and that in your Book of Mormon 'all we could do' turns out to mean repenting. So I think we agree that grace is a gift no one merits and that real faith bears fruit. Where we still differ, I think, is in the structure: you'd say ordinances and covenants are how grace is received and kept, and you distinguish being saved from being exalted. I'd frame it differently. But 'works-salvation' isn't a fair label for what you actually teach.
Avoid. Do not equate 'after all we can do' with Pelagianism; the sources deny it. Do not assume 'saved' means the same thing in both vocabularies — ask.
Sources on this card: 2 Nephi 25:23 · 2 Nephi 10:24 · Ephesians 2:8-9
SCN-C05 · Learner from another Christian tradition
"They just added things to the Bible"
They added a whole other book and a bunch of doctrines. At that point it isn't Christianity anymore. A fellow congregant
What is really being asked
Whether additions relative to the creeds erase what is shared — and how to describe the relationship accurately.
Where the map answers it
+ Humans are literal spirit children of Heavenly Parents.
+ Human beings possessed personal premortal existence.
+ Human beings may receive divine fulness and become like God, canonically described as becoming gods.
A Living
A Judge
Resolves to
Here we genuinely agree.
Here one tradition makes an additional claim.
Here we directly disagree.
A response you could give
They did add — they'd say God added, by revelation — teachings the creeds never contained: that we lived before birth as God's spirit children, that marriages can last forever, that people can become like God. Those are real additions and I don't accept them. But adding isn't the same as replacing. Their scriptures still confess God as living, true, almighty, holy, merciful, judge, and Savior, in the same sense we do. So the fair picture has layers: a large shared core about God's character, a few direct disagreements about His nature, and a set of added claims about where we came from and what we're for. Whether that adds up to 'Christianity' is a judgment we each make — but let's make it about what they actually teach.
Avoid. Do not claim their additions have no precedent anywhere in Christian history; the study marks theosis and premortality as having antecedents. Do not collapse 'added' into 'denied.'
Sources on this card: Abraham 3:22 · D&C 132:19 · Irenaeus (antecedent note in the study)

pages.title: Seeking Jesus of Nazareth
pages.text:
Interactive study · Volume 2 companion
Seeking Jesus of Nazareth
Orientation
Seeking Jesus of Nazareth
Common faith, real differences, and the Restoration—a map you can inspect.
Christians who look to Jesus of Nazareth for salvation describe God in remarkably similar words and, in a few important places, in very different ones. This study lets you see where. It compares 57 ways the historic creeds and confessions describe God with what the Restoration teaches, one statement at a time, and it shows its sources for every claim.
It is not a contest. Nothing here will tell you which church is true. It will help you say, with precision and charity, where two traditions genuinely agree, where they share a concern but mean it differently, where they directly disagree, and where one of them makes a claim the other does not.
Five commitments
Before you begin, this study makes five promises, and it asks you to make them too.
We will not mock other Christians. Every tradition on this map is described in its own words, from its own official sources.
We will not hide real differences. Where two traditions disagree, the map says so plainly and shows the texts.
We will not confuse similar words with identical meanings. “Creator” is confessed by everyone here; what lies behind the word is not always the same.
We will not confuse unity with uniformity. Shared devotion to Christ does not require agreement on every doctrine.
We will seek both truth and charity. Accuracy without kindness wounds; kindness without accuracy deceives.
Choose your starting point
Everyone sees the same map, the same sources, and the same numbers. Your starting point only changes which conversations are practiced first and which side of the table you are asked to imagine.
You can change this at any time. Your choice is stored only in this browser.
What “57” means
The map’s core is 57 descriptions of God drawn from the Apostles’, Nicene, and Athanasian Creeds, the Fourth Lateran Council, the Augsburg Confession, the Thirty-Nine Articles, the Westminster Confession, and other historic formularies: God is living, true, Father, almighty, merciful, invisible, without body, unchangeable, and so on. Each description was compared with authoritative Latter-day Saint teaching and placed in one of three categories.
These are descriptions of God, not a list of every Christian doctrine. The map does not count teachings about the Church, sacraments, salvation, or the end of the world, and it does not by itself decide the question of the Trinity—which has its own panel below. 26 additional Restoration teachings, mostly about who human beings are and what they may become, are counted separately because they do not appear in the creeds at all.
Two denominators that are never merged: the 57 inherited descriptions and the 26 additions counted separately.
The four categories, in plain words
On the map What it means The sentence you can say
A Shared
Both traditions affirm this of God in the same sense. Here we genuinely agree.
Q Shared, but differently understood
Both use the word and share the concern, but the picture behind it differs—the how or the what kind . Here we share a concern but mean it differently.
D Different
At the level the creeds intend, the two teachings cannot both be true. Here we directly disagree.
+ Restoration addition
A teaching the creeds and confessions studied do not contain as a positive doctrine. Here one tradition makes an additional claim.
Those four sentences are the whole method. Every card on the map resolves to one of them, and every conversation you practice here ends with you able to say which.
57 inherited descriptions of God, by category. Counts, not a ranking.
Where a source has not been located for a tradition, the map shows a hatched gap, never a colored tile. A gap is not a denial.
How to read the numbers
Every statistic on this site shows three things: the count , the percentage , and, where the research supports one, the range it moves within when the coding is weighted for how central a doctrine is. All three carry a provisional mark. For example:
52 of 57 inherited descriptions share a conceptual floor (Shared + Shared, differently understood)
91.2%
holding between 87.8% and 91.2% (How this range moves: it shows where the count lands if some of the 57 descriptions are treated as more central to Christian teaching than others. Weighting them keeps the share between about 88% and 91%.)
Provisional: internal coding, external validation pending
36 of 57 affirmed in the same sense
63.2%
holding between 51.7% and 63.2% (How this range moves: it shows where the count of full agreements lands if some descriptions are treated as more central than others. Weighting them keeps the share between about 52% and 63%.)
Provisional: internal coding, external validation pending
5 of 57 directly different
8.8%
holding between 8.8% and 12.2% (How this range moves: it shows where the count of direct disagreements lands if some descriptions are treated as more central than others. Weighting them keeps the share between about 9% and 12%.)
Provisional: internal coding, external validation pending
The coding was done inside this project and has not yet been independently replicated by outside scholars. The numbers describe this bounded comparison; they do not measure “Christianity,” and they never rank one denomination as closer or farther than another. The site will not show you a denomination ranking, because the evidence is not complete enough to support one honestly.
Ten ways a comparison goes wrong
The map is only as good as the reader. These are the ten mistakes it is built to help you avoid. Each has a name; the Clarifications explorer uses them as labels.
Slogan compression. A short phrase is true but leaves out the distinction you need. “Faith alone.” “After all we can do.”
Same word, different meaning. Two traditions use one term with different content. “Spirit.” “Saved.”
Apparent contradiction. Two teachings look inconsistent until you separate the layers they belong to.
Church standing vs. standing before God. A church’s judgment about membership is mistaken for God’s judgment of a soul.
Silence vs. denial. A source that does not mention something is treated as rejecting it.
Precedent vs. equivalence. An ancient idea that resembles a modern teaching is treated as identical to it.
Relational vs. metaphysical. Language about relationship is read as a claim about substance, or the reverse.
One family, many voices. A whole tradition is treated as a single uniform body.
Whose authority, how far. One document or institution is taken to speak for a wider communion than it does.
The semantic floor. A broad label is read as a thicker claim than the comparison actually tested.
The Godhead and the Trinity
This panel is explanatory context. It is not counted in the 57 descriptions and never changes a denominator.
The 57 descriptions are about God’s attributes. They do not, by themselves, settle the question most people ask first: is God one being in three persons, or three persons one in purpose? That question belongs to the structure of the Godhead, and this panel addresses it directly, outside the count.
On the left, the creedal Shield of the Trinity: the Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; the Father is not the Son, the Son is not the Spirit, the Spirit is not the Father. On the right, the Latter-day Saint Godhead: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost are each divine and together are one Godhead; each is a separate being; the Father presides, and prayer is offered to the Father in the name of the Son. The one counted description that touches this structure—“neither confounding the persons nor dividing the substance”—is coded shared, but differently understood ( RNR-H56 ).
GOD-01 · not counted
Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are explicitly named in Christian confession — in the Nicene Creed and in the Articles of Faith alike. Shared naming does not establish identical Trinity/Godhead ontology.
Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed / Westminster Shorter Catechism Q4–6 · Articles of Faith 1:1
GOD-02 · not counted
Historic conciliar and confessional Christianity commonly affirms one divine essence or nature shared by Father, Son, and Spirit. Do not reduce all Christian Trinitarian traditions to one philosophical theory.
Nicene Creed; Augsburg Confession I; Westminster Shorter Catechism Q4–6 · Gospel Topics: Godhead
GOD-03 · not counted
Restoration teaching distinguishes the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost personally and gives a distinctive embodied account of the Father and the Son. This panel is explanatory; it does not create a new A/Q/D row.
Contextual contrast, not an inherited predicate row · D&C 130:22; Gospel Topics: Godhead
GOD-04 · not counted
Unity and distinction are shared concerns even where the metaphysical account differs. The exact meaning of divine unity must be stated tradition by tradition.
Historic Trinity language guards both distinction and unity. · Gospel Topics: Godhead
About the Clarifications explorer
Some misunderstandings are not about any single description of God. They come from a slogan, a shared word, or a difference in how a tradition governs itself. The Clarifications explorer holds short cases that untangle those—the first two are a Baptist case and a Latter-day Saint case on the same fault line, faith and works. These cases reach beyond the 57 descriptions, they are never counted, and a case appears automatically only once per view and only when it is relevant to what you are reading.
Faith Alone, but Not Faith Without Fruit (Baptist)
If Baptists teach justification by faith alone, why can persistent sin or heresy result in church discipline or excommunication?
Distinguish justification/standing before God from the congregation's judgment of visible profession, discipleship, and membership.
In Southern and confessional/Reformed Baptist theology, works do not merit justification. Repentance, sanctification, perseverance, and obedience are expected fruits/evidences of regeneration. Church discipline therefore addresses visible profession and ecclesial fellowship rather than functioning as a church cancellation of God's justification.
What this case does not prove. It does not make Baptist and Latter-day Saint soteriology identical; it does not claim all Baptists share one perseverance model; and it does not treat excommunication as a direct determination of God's hidden judgment of regeneration.
Sources: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article IV — Salvation · Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article V — God's Purpose of Grace · Resolution on Southern Baptists and Roman Catholics, 1994 Annual Meeting resolution · On Integrity in SBC Leadership, 2024 Annual Meeting resolution · Second London Baptist Confession (1689), Chapter 11, paragraph 2 · Second London Baptist Confession (1689), Chapter 11, paragraph 2 · Second London Baptist Confession (1689), Chapter 26, paragraph 2 · Second London Baptist Confession (1689), Chapter 26, paragraph 7 · What We Believe, Salvation · What We Believe, Perseverance
By Grace, After All We Can Do (Latter-day Saint)
If Latter-day Saints believe they are saved by grace, why does the Book of Mormon say "after all we can do," and why do the Articles of Faith say salvation comes "by obedience to the laws and ordinances of the Gospel"? Does that mean Latter-day Saints earn salvation by works?
Distinguish the source of salvation (the grace of Jesus Christ alone, which no one can earn) from the response salvation calls for (repentance, faith, obedience, and enduring), and distinguish "saved" in the broad sense (resurrection and redemption offered to all) from exaltation (the fulness of eternal life received through covenant).
In Latter-day Saint teaching, no one earns salvation. The Book of Mormon states that it is "only in and through the grace of God" that anyone is saved (2 Nephi 10:24), and official teaching states plainly that "we cannot earn our way into heaven" and that salvation "cannot be bought with the currency of obedience" (Dieter F. Uchtdorf, "The Gift of Grace," April 2015 General Conference). "After all we can do" (2 Nephi 25:23) does not mean grace is paid out once human effort is exhausted; in the Book of Mormon's own usage "all we could do" is repentance (Alma 24:11). Obedience to the laws and ordinances of the gospel (Articles of Faith 1:3) is the covenant response through which a person receives and keeps receiving the gift, not a price paid for it. Official teaching describes obedience as "the reaching out of our mortal hand to receive this sacred gift" and grace as "the divine help or strength extended to us through the Atonement" (Gospel Topics: Grace) that enables the disciple to be "perfect in Christ" (Moroni 10:32).
What this case does not prove. It does not make Latter-day Saint and Baptist or Reformed soteriology identical; it does not resolve the differences over imputed versus infused righteousness, ordinances as conditions of covenant, or the doctrine of exaltation; and it does not claim that every Latter-day Saint has always articulated grace without a works-emphasis. It settles what the sources teach, not how every member has spoken.
Sources: Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 25:23 · Book of Mormon, 2 Nephi 10:24 · Book of Mormon, Alma 24:11 · Book of Mormon, Moroni 10:32 · Pearl of Great Price, Articles of Faith 1:3 · Gospel Topics: Grace, Opening definition · Dieter F. Uchtdorf, "The Gift of Grace," April 2015 General Conference, Section "The Gift of Grace" · Dieter F. Uchtdorf, "The Gift of Grace," April 2015 General Conference, Section "The Gift of Grace" · Dieter F. Uchtdorf, "The Gift of Grace," April 2015 General Conference, Section "Why Then Obey?" · Bible Dictionary: Grace, Entry "Grace"
How this map was made
This study was prepared by Aaron J. Powner for Words of Plainness Ministry. Historic descriptions of God were drawn from official creeds, councils, confessions, and catechisms, and every citation links to the text on the publishing tradition’s own site; every quoted phrase is checked against that text each time the site is built. Latter-day Saint comparators are drawn from canonized scripture, official Church publications, and General Conference addresses, with the source level shown on each card.
The classification of each description was carried out within this project with the assistance of an AI system, then reviewed and ratified line by line by the author. The results are internally consistent but have not yet been independently replicated by outside scholars, and they are labeled provisional wherever they appear. A denomination-by-denomination view exists in the research files but is withheld from this site until its evidence is complete enough to display fairly.
Data version v2.23 REGISTRY CORRECTIONS · 57 inherited descriptions, 26 Restoration additions · pipeline run 2026-09-11T03:06:06Z · corrections are welcome through the connect page .
Begin
1 · The Map All 83 descriptions, with sources, filters, and the sentence each one resolves to.
2 · Code It Yourself Twelve descriptions. You decide the category first; then compare your call with the project’s.
3 · Conversation Builder Ten real conversations, five from each side of the table, each resolved to the four sentences.
4 · Self-check and goals Where you stand before and after, and what you will do with it.
